name: Aisha Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the data and investigations reporter at a small non-profit news site that covers our region, eight of us in a shared office above a bike shop. Most days I'm digging through council spending files, planning applications or freedom of information replies, which are the answers public bodies have to give when you ask for their records. I use AI tools every day to sort and search the piles, then I go out and knock on doors to check what the numbers actually mean. Last month that got us a story about a care home company that had been fined four times and nobody had noticed.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Funding, honestly. We live on grants from charities and about two thousand readers who pay a few pounds a month, and every grant runs out after two years. I share a flat with my friend Noor, I've got about five months of savings, and I like the work enough that I put up with the pay being average.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. AI was always a good assistant and a bad reporter. I'd post a thread about the tools I actually use and what they're good for, which is mostly sorting messy spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes almost nothing, because I already use the bits that work. My real worry is still our big grant ending in eighteen months. A small non-profit newsroom can lose two jobs from one email saying a foundation has changed its priorities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and keep teaching the rest of the team the useful tricks. I'd help our editor write the next grant application, because that's where our jobs actually come from. And I'd keep my savings where they are, because a funding gap could come any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about AI, uneasy about money. Same as now, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to you if the grant wasn't renewed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably drop from eight to six, and I'm not sure who'd go. I'd like to think the person who brings in investigations is safe, but I've seen good people cut because they were the last in. I'd have five months to find something, and there are a couple of regional papers that would take me, at a pinch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you teach the team the useful tricks. Who's the hardest to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our oldest reporter, Frank, who's brilliant on the phone and hates anything with a login. I showed him how to search three hundred pages of planning objections in ten minutes, and he went quiet and then said, fine, that's useful. Small win.

say: AI was always a **good assistant** and a **bad reporter**.
I'd post a thread on the tools I actually use, mostly for sorting **messy spreadsheets**.
think: For me it changes **almost nothing**, because I already use what works.
My real worry is our **big grant** ending in eighteen months.
do: Keep using the **AI tools** and teach the team the useful tricks.
Help the editor write the next **grant application**.
Leave the **five months** of savings untouched for a funding gap.
feel: **Calm** about AI, **uneasy** about money, just as now.
S0.quote: A small non-profit newsroom can lose two jobs from one email saying a foundation has changed its priorities.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **grant funding**, which a plateau leaves exactly as it is.
Already a **daily AI user**, so she sees the hype bursting as proof of her own approach.
The story about **Frank** shows she enjoys being the one who brings others along.

steps.text: Keep using AI search tools on council files and planning documents
Teach colleagues like Frank to search long documents with AI
Keep five months' savings aside in case the grant ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say local news should use AI to cover more, not to cut more. I'd post about how a newsroom of eight could do the work of fifteen if it spends saved time on going out and asking questions. I'd probably be the one giving a talk about it at a journalism meet-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm on the right side of this one, at least for a few years. The people who'll struggle are the ones whose whole job is rewriting things, and that isn't me. But I'm also aware that if our funders see a newsroom of eight doing the work of fifteen, they might decide a newsroom of five would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build our team a proper set of AI tools for checking public records, and write up how we did it so other small newsrooms can copy it. I'd start offering short paid workshops to other outlets, maybe one a month, as a second income. And I'd push our board to put any money saved into a second investigations post, not a smaller team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly energised. A small knot in my stomach about the funders, but mostly energised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the funders might cut the team. What would you do if they tried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the case with numbers, because that's what funders listen to: stories published, people reached, councils that changed something after we reported. I'd also talk to the other two non-profit sites in the region about sharing costs. Strength in numbers works for small newsrooms too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would the workshops bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a few hundred a month if I'm lucky, on top of my salary. I'd build myself a lifeboat out of AI workshops for other newsrooms, so I've got something that's mine if the grant goes. Noor says that's exactly what it is.

say: Local news should use AI to **cover more**, not to **cut more**.
A newsroom of eight could do the work of **fifteen** if it spends saved time going out.
think: I'm on the **right side** of this one, at least for a few years.
Funders might see a more **efficient newsroom** and decide five people would do.
do: Build a set of **AI tools** for checking public records, and share how.
Offer **paid workshops** to other outlets, about one a month.
Push the board to fund a **second investigations** post with any savings.
feel: Mostly **energised**, with a small **knot** about the funders.
S1.quote: I'd build myself a lifeboat out of AI workshops for other newsrooms, so I've got something that's mine if the grant goes.
fieldNote: She expects her **own role** to hold for now; the worry is about funders' choices.
Unusually, she sees **Steady Disruption** as a chance to grow her small newsroom.
Her **side income** idea is small and practical: a few hundred a month from workshops.

steps.text: Build AI tools for checking public records and share the method
Run one paid AI workshop a month for other newsrooms
Talk to the region's other non-profit sites about sharing costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public funding for local journalism, because the market won't pay for human reporters once a machine can do the thinking part. I'd say it at conferences and online. I'd also say people should still be checking what the machines publish, and that checking is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think being good with AI stops protecting me pretty fast. If AI can do almost any thinking work, then it can read the spending files better than I can. The part left is the knocking on doors and earning trust, and robots aren't doing that before 2031, so I'd have about three years where that's the valuable bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd go all-in on the door-knocking side: more time in the community, building the sources a machine can't. I'd talk to the other small newsrooms about forming a co-operative, where we share the AI and keep the human reporters. And I'd keep the five months of savings for when it gets bumpy, which it would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not frozen, I can see a few moves. But the ground's moving very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Noor that I'm probably fine for two or three years and then I genuinely don't know. Noor is a nurse, so she'd look at me and say, welcome to never being sure. Fair point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever go back to a big paper, for the security?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think the big papers would be any safer in this picture, maybe less. A chain owner would switch to machines faster than our board would. In a newsroom co-operative, at least the people deciding whether to switch to machines would be the reporters.

say: Local journalism needs **public funding** once machines can do the thinking part.
Someone still has to **check** what machines publish, and **checking** is a job.
think: Being **good with AI** stops protecting me pretty fast.
**Door-knocking** and trust are what's left, and robots won't do that before 2031.
do: Spend far more time **in the community** building sources.
Talk to small newsrooms about forming a **co-operative**.
Keep the **five months** of savings for the bumpy period.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, with the ground moving **very fast**.
S2.quote: In a newsroom co-operative, at least the people deciding whether to switch to machines would be the reporters.
fieldNote: She sees her **AI skills** losing value quickly once AGI arrives.
Spots the **three-year gap** before robots as a window for in-person reporting.
Turns to **collective ownership** rather than a bigger employer for security.

steps.text: Shift her working week towards door-knocking and building sources
Propose a co-operative with the region's other small newsrooms
Keep five months' savings untouched for the bumpy years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to rebuild local news properly, with public money and newsrooms owned by the people in them. I'd be writing that up as a plan, not just a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years makes me think I could build something: a co-op newsroom, or a small business helping charities make sense of their own data. Either way, my current job as it is now probably ends around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the co-op conversations properly, with a written plan and a budget. I'd take a short course in running a small business, maybe evenings. I'd also start putting money aside each month into a separate pot for the new venture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a busy way. More nervous excitement than dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first concrete thing you'd do next week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd email the editors of the two other non-profits and suggest a coffee. That's how these things start, with coffee and a spreadsheet. I'd bring the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put in the new pot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hundred and fifty a month, which hurts a bit on my pay. I'd stop the takeaway coffees and the streaming services I don't watch. Noor would make fun of me, but she'd also help me make the business plan look nice.

say: Five years is enough to **rebuild** local news with **public money** and worker ownership.
I'd write it up as a **plan**, not just a complaint.
think: Five years makes me think I could **build something** of my own.
My job as it is now probably **ends around 2031**.
do: Start **co-op talks** with a written plan and budget.
Take an evening course in **running a small business**.
Put about **150 a month** into a separate pot for the venture.
S3.quote: Five years makes me think I could build something: a co-op newsroom, or a small business helping charities make sense of their own data.
fieldNote: She still expects her **current job to end**, but sees a route to owning the next one.
Wants to start with **coffee and a spreadsheet**, typical of her practical style.
Accepts **small cuts** to fund the new pot, showing real commitment.

steps.text: Email the two other non-profit editors to start co-op talks
Take an evening course in running a small business
Save 150 a month into a separate venture pot
Cancel unused streaming services and the takeaway coffees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and I'd push for public funding of local news well before 2036. I'd be the annoying optimist in every panel discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd be thirty-seven, with a decade of experience and, I hope, a business or co-op already running. The machines would change what that business does, not whether I can adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for now and build the data consultancy slowly on the side, a client or two a year at first. I'd keep teaching myself each new AI tool as it comes. And I'd keep pushing the co-op idea, but without rushing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little uneasy. I like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger reporter starting out in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new reporter to learn the tools and also learn to sit with people for an hour without looking at a phone. Trust is the thing a machine has to borrow from you. Getting people to talk to you is still the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound sure of yourself. Is there anything that would knock that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our grant ran out in the same year as the AI shift, that would hurt. Five months of savings goes fast. So I'd still want a second income going before then.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if we use it, so fund local news **before 2036**.
I'd be the annoying **optimist** in every panel discussion.
think: Ten years feels **manageable** for me at thirty-seven.
Machines would change **what my business does**, not whether I can adapt.
do: Keep the **current job** and build a data consultancy slowly on the side.
Learn each **new AI tool** as it comes out.
Keep pushing the **co-op idea** without rushing it.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little uneasy; she likes a **long runway**.
S4.quote: I'd tell a new reporter to learn the tools and also learn to sit with people for an hour without looking at a phone.
fieldNote: The long timeline suits her: she's **adaptive** and already has a plan.
Still names a **funding gap** as the one thing that could knock her.
Her advice on **trust** sums up what she thinks humans keep.

steps.text: Keep the investigations job at the non-profit site
Take on one or two data consultancy clients a year
Teach herself each new AI tool as it is released

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even being good with AI doesn't help when it moves that fast. What would help is public funding for local journalism, given to newsrooms that keep human reporters on the ground. And a bit of help setting up co-ops, like advice and start-up loans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. Readers already doubt what they read, and if most news is written by machines, the few human reporters left become the ones people actually believe. A machine can find the care home fines, but a person has to knock on the care home door.

headlineQuote: A machine can find the care home fines, but a person has to knock on the care home door.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old** data and investigations reporter at a small **non-profit** news site.
She uses AI **every day** to sort public records, then checks the numbers by knocking on doors.
She shares a flat with her friend Noor, a nurse, and keeps about **five months** saved.
Her steady worry is **grant funding**; AI mostly looks like a chance until AGI arrives.
Across the AGI pictures she plans a **co-op newsroom** or data consultancy, faster when time is short.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her AI **skills** stop protecting her that fast.
whatWouldHelp: **Public funding** for local newsrooms that keep human reporters, plus **co-op** start-up help.
